title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates the canonical operational guidance for Redwood's serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel scheduling rationale, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes highlights, known issues, and on-call runbooks. Intended audience: runtime engineers, platform SREs, performance reviewers, and on-call responders.

Goals
- Maintain predictable latency under production workloads (P95 and P99 SLOs).
- Maximize throughput / GPU utilization while respecting latency SLOs.
- Provide repeatable profiling and benchmarking processes for regressions and onboarding new kernels or quantized model variants.
- Ensure clear runbooks for common incidents (OOMs, GPU hangs, tail latency spikes).

1) High-level runtime architecture
--------------------------------
Summary: The serving runtime is composed of the following logical components: dispatcher, request router, scheduling layer, kernel-selection engine, execution agents (GPU workers), KV cache service, model artifact manager, and telemetry/observability pipeline.

Components
- Dispatcher & ingress: HTTP/gRPC front door with per-tenant rate limiting and request normalization.
- Router & policy engine: routes requests by policy (latency, cost, region, tenant tier).
- Scheduler: decides batching boundaries, GPU affinity, and kernel variant selection.
- Execution agents (workers): host model shards or full-model replicas; expose IPC for batch submission.
- Kernel selection & runtime compiler: chooses optimized kernels based on model metadata, sequence length, and hardware profile.
- KV cache store: per-tenant prefix cache for KV reuse across requests.
- Model repo & versioning: serves model artifacts and quantization metadata to workers.
- Telemetry: tracing, per-token metrics, heatmaps, and profiler hooks.

SLOs & Targets (global defaults)
- P95 latency: <= 200ms for short-text generation (<=128 tokens).
- P99 latency: <= 400ms for short-text generation.
- Throughput target: tokens/sec per GPU varies by model; target 1.0x of baseline for each new kernel release.
- Error budget: 0.5% monthly error rate for 5xx responses.

Ownership
- Runtime architecture & scheduler: eng-serving-runtime team (primary).
- Telemetry & alerting: eng-platform (secondary).
- Kernel compilation & perf testing: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals.

2) Kernel scheduling: design and configuration
------------------------------------------------
Design goals
- Minimize tail latency by avoiding unbounded batching for latency-sensitive requests.
- Maximize batching for cost-sensitive and high-throughput workloads.
- Select kernels that optimize for current seq_len distribution and hardware (FP16, INT8/4 quantized kernels).

Scheduling primitives
- Priority class: latency | standard | background.
- Max batch size: configured per-model and per-gpu-type.
- Age threshold: maximum time a request may wait in queue before forced flush (ms).
- Sequence-length bucketing: group requests by requested generation length to reduce wasted computation.
- Preemption: latency class preempts background batches when SLO risk detected.

Typical configuration table (example)
| parameter            | latency class | standard class | background class | notes |
|----------------------|---------------|----------------|------------------|-------|
| max_batch_size       | 8             | 64             | 256              | tuned per GPU type |
| age_threshold_ms     | 8             | 30             | 100              | lower -> lower tail latency |
| seq_bucket_cutoffs   | 32,128        | 64,256         | 256+             | used to choose kernel variant |
| gpu_affinity         | exclusive     | shared         | shared            | exclusive reduces contention |

Heuristics and rules of thumb
- If P99 > 2x target, reduce max_batch_size by 50% for latency class.
- When average KV cache hit rate > 30%, increase background batch size to leverage reuse.
- For seq_len distribution with > 20% long requests (>512), prefer kernels optimized for long sequences even if they slightly reduce short-seq throughput.

3) Profiling playbook (how to reproduce and triage perf regressions)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
When to run: suspected regression from CI, alert from perf dashboards, or customer report of latency/throughput degradation.

Step-by-step profiling checklist
1. Reproduce the problem in the perf lab or a staging fleet that mirrors prod traffic patterns (use the same traffic shape: prompt set, tokens, arrival rate).
2. Collect system-level metrics: nvidia-smi (GPU utilization, memory), top / pidstat (CPU), network stats, and disk IO.
3. Enable runtime tracing for a small subset of requests (sample 0.1%): capture scheduler decisions, batching sizes, kernel variant, and latency per stage (ingress, queue, kernel, postprocess).
4. Run kernel-level profilers: nsight-systems or Nsight Compute for CUDA kernels; for ROCm use rocprof. For PyTorch operator-level profiling use torch.profiler.
5. Gather kernel selection logs and compare with baseline (previous good release).
6. If TLS/serialization overhead is suspected, capture request/response sizes and decode/encode latency.

Essential commands (examples)
- Collect GPU summary:
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 2
- Run Nsight Systems capture (30s):
  - nsight-sys --capture-range=preset:statement --trace=cuda,cudnn -o /tmp/trace.qdrep -- python3 stress_client.py --target <worker_ip> --qps 50
- PyTorch operator profiling snippet:
  - from torch.profiler import profile, record_function, ProfilerActivity
  - with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], record_shapes=True) as prof:
      ... run sample inference ...
  - print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", row_limit=20))

Profiling outputs to collect
- kernel flamegraphs (Nsight output)
- timeline traces (scheduler + runtime stages)
- per-op latencies and memory alloc/free patterns
- GPU SM occupancy and memory stalls
- RPC/IPC latencies between dispatcher and worker

Common root causes and quick fixes
- Memory fragmentation / excessive allocs: enable pooling, reduce ephemeral allocations, or increase reserved memory pool.
- Bad kernel chosen for seq_len distribution: adjust kernel-selection thresholds or add new kernel variant.
- Large serialization overhead: switch to zero-copy path or increase batch size for that tenant.

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
--------------------------------------
Purpose: provide repeatable, automated perf regression testing for kernel updates, quantization changes, and scheduler tunings.

Benchmarks included
- Microbenchmarks: single-batch latency for common seq lengths (1, 32, 128, 512).
- Throughput benchmarks: sustained tokens/sec for pinned GPUs at target batch shapes.
- End-to-end workload: synthetic traces matching prod arrival patterns (burstiness, mix of short/long requests).
- Cost-aware runs: effective tokens-per-dollar calculated using instance pricing.

Test harness and artifacts
- stress_client.py: driver that replays prompt sets with configurable QPS, parallelism, and client-side timers.
- baseline-configs/: JSON workloads for each model / hw profile.
- results/: Stores CSV with metrics (P50, P95, P99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU_util, mem_used).
- golden_baselines/: approved performance metrics for each supported kernel/model.

CI gating policy
- New kernel or runtime change must run the full benchmark suite on a dedicated perf cluster.
- Regression thresholds: P95 must not regress > 10% vs golden baseline; tokens/sec must not regress > 7%.
- If threshold exceeded, auto-fail the PR and open a performance triage issue assigned to eng-serving-runtime.

Reproducibility checklist
- Capture seed, protobuf payloads, exact model artifact commit hash, runtime build id, kernel binaries, and GPU driver versions.
- Store collected artifacts alongside benchmark results in the perf artifact store.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)
----------------------------------
Release: runtime v2026.02.10 (runtime binary 1.12.0)
- Kernel selection: added dynamic seq-length bucketer and fallthrough kernel that reduces overall P99 by ~14% on A100.
- Quantization: improved INT8 fallback path for Gemm kernels; reduced per-token memory by 22% for 2B-class models.
- Scheduler: new preemption window to favor latency class requests when tail latency risk is detected.
- Observability: added per-kernel heatmaps and aggregated per-tenant token cost metrics.
- Fixes: resolved intermittent GPU OOM during autoregressive decoding for long-context workloads (see issue RT-1493).

Release: runtime v2025.12.01 (runtime binary 1.10.4)
- Initial support for continuous batching across multi-tenant scenarios.
- Improved serialization zero-copy path for gRPC clients.

For full changelog see related page: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes-2026

6) Known issues (active)
------------------------
- RT-1529: Occasional P99 spikes on mixed short/long workloads when cache hit rate oscillates. Impact: sporadic latency degradations for standard-class requests. Mitigation: temporarily set stricter age_threshold_ms for standard class; assigned to Priya Raman.
- RT-1493: Rare GPU OOM during long autoregressive decoding on INT8 kernels (occurs when KV cache grows unexpectedly). Impact: 5xx errors for some long-request customers. Mitigation: enforce max_kv_cache_entries per-tenant and trigger eviction earlier; owner: Miguel Torres.
- RT-1578: Nsight capture causes 5-10% slowdown when run on production-similar clusters; use staging perf cluster for heavy profiler captures.

If adding new known issues: follow the template -> id, summary, impact, workaround, owner, target fix release.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
-----------------------------------------
A. High tail latency (P99 spikes)
1. Confirm alert & scope: check dashboards (per-model, per-tenant P95/P99) and identify affected model/tenant.
2. Collect traces for affected period (enable higher sampling for 5-10 minutes).
3. Check scheduler metrics: average batch size, age_threshold breaches, preemption events.
4. If batch sizes are too large for latency class, reduce max_batch_size and age_threshold for that class.
5. If kernel mismatch suspected, force kernel variant to last-known-good for that model and observe.
6. If changes mitigate, document and roll out controlled fix.

B. GPU out-of-memory (OOM) during decode
1. Identify worker and model artifact (logs show OOM and stack).
2. If transient, restart worker and observe. If repeated, place worker in maintenance and re-route traffic.
3. Reduce concurrency on that worker (set worker.capacity to 0.5x) and increase reserved memory pool.
4. Investigate KV cache size: trim per-tenant cache entries; if needed enable eviction for long contexts.
5. Owner: escalation to eng-serving-runtime on-call.

C. GPU hang / driver crash
1. Drain the node (mark unschedulable), failover requests to healthy nodes.
2. Capture driver logs and coredump.
3. File incident with infra (eng-infra) and attach Nsight capture if available.
4. Reimage node per infra playbook; if recurrence, quarantine GPU and open hardware ticket.

D. Degraded throughput (tokens/sec drop)
1. Verify upstream QPS and client-side behavior.
2. Check GPU utilization (if low, likely scheduling inefficiency).
3. Inspect batch shapes and age thresholds; increase aggregation for background workloads if safe.
4. If utilization high but throughput low, profile kernel for stalls or memory thrashing.

Playbook ownership and escalation
- On-call owner: eng-serving-runtime pager (primary).
- Escalation: eng-platform -> eng-infra -> applied-ml-and-evals for kernel regressions.
- Contact list: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com, infra-oncall@redwood.example.com, perf-team@redwood.example.com

8) Team wiki and operational hygiene
----------------------------------
Recommended pages to keep updated (owners in parentheses)
- runtime-architecture-and-profiling-playbook (Asha Patel)
- kernel-selection-guidelines (Miguel Torres)
- perf-benchmarks-and-golden-baselines (Ethan Liu)
- release-notes (eng-serving-runtime)
- incident-runbooks (eng-sre)

Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers
1. Read this playbook and associated architecture docs.
2. Run the microbenchmark suite locally and compare to golden baseline.
3. Shadow on-call for two weeks and run at least one post-incident review.
4. Contribute at least one perf test or kernel optimization to the baseline.

Maintenance cadence
- Weekly: telemetry review - check P95/P99 and any new unexpected regressions.
- Biweekly: perf benchmark runs on stable perf cluster for active branches.
- Quarterly: review golden baselines and update kernel selection thresholds after major model changes.
